hero.title: The Crown Rule (1858-1947)
hero.description: Master the constitutional and legislative evolution of India under the British Crown, from the Government of India Act 1858 to the Indian Independence Act 1947 (UPSC GS Paper-2: Constitutional Development).

mockIntro.title: Interactive UPSC Mock Test
mockIntro.description: Assess your understanding of the Indian Councils Acts, diarchy, provincial autonomy, and constitutional transition. This timed test contains 10 high-yield, exam-standard questions with negative marking.

timeline.title: Chronological Milestones of Crown Rule
timeline.description: Key legislative changes marking the constitutional evolution under the British Crown.

cards.details: Transferred power from EIC to British Crown. Created office of Secretary of State for India and designated Governor-General as Viceroy (Lord Canning).
Initiated decentralization by restoring legislative powers to Bombay/Madras. Introduced portfolio system and Viceroy's ordinance-making power.
Expanded non-official members, allowed legislative councils to discuss budget and address questions to executive. Introduced indirect elections.
Indian Councils Act 1909. Introduced separate electorates for Muslims (legalizing communalism). Added Satyendra Prasad Sinha to Viceroy's Executive Council.
Government of India Act 1919. Introduced diarchy in provinces, bicameralism at center, direct elections, and paved way for Central Public Service Commission (1926).
Proposed All-India Federation. Abolished provincial diarchy, introduced provincial autonomy, and established Federal Court (1937) and RBI.
Abolished office of Viceroy and Secretary of State. Declared Constituent Assemblies sovereign bodies, ending British rule on August 15, 1947.

mnemonics.title: Mnemonics & Memory Hacks
mnemonics.description: Visual hooks to memorize complex details of the Crown Rule Acts for UPSC.

items.title: Mnemonic 1: Indian Councils Act of 1861
items.decryption: Remember 1861 provisions: **Viceroy** Canning nominates Indians; **Devolves** power (restores Bombay/Madras legislative powers); Viceroy gets **Ordinance** powers; **Portfolio** system legalized.

items.title: Mnemonic 2: Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909
items.decryption: Remember 1909 provisions: Satyendra **Sinha** joins Executive Council; **Separate** electorate for Muslims; **Sixty** members in Central Legislative Council (increased from 16); **Morley** (SoS) and Minto (Viceroy) reforms.

items.title: Mnemonic 3: Mont-Ford Reforms of 1919
items.decryption: Remember 1919 provisions: **Diarchy** in provinces; **B**icameralism at the center; **D**irect elections introduced; **D**evolution of budgets (provincial separated from central).

items.title: Mnemonic 4: Government of India Act of 1935
items.decryption: Remember 1935 provisions: All-India **Federation** proposed; **Opens** Federal Court & **Reserve** Bank of India; **Provincial Autonomy** introduced (dyarchy abolished in provinces, introduced at center).

flashcards.title: Active Recall Flashcards
flashcards.description: Quick active recall drill to test legislative facts before attempting practice questions.

items.question: Which act designated the Governor-General of India as the Viceroy, and who was the first Viceroy?
items.answer: The Government of India Act 1858 designated the GG as the Viceroy. Lord Canning was the first Viceroy of India.

items.question: Which act legalized the 'Portfolio System' in Indian administration?
items.answer: The Indian Councils Act of 1861 gave statutory recognition to the portfolio system introduced by Lord Canning in 1859.

items.question: Under which act was budget discussion allowed in the Legislative Councils for the first time?
items.answer: The Indian Councils Act of 1892 allowed members to discuss the budget and address questions to the executive.

items.question: Who is known as the 'Father of Communal Electorate' in India and why?
items.answer: Lord Minto, because he introduced separate electorates for Muslims under the Indian Councils Act 1909.

items.question: By which act was 'Diarchy' introduced in the provinces, and by which act was it replaced with 'Provincial Autonomy'?
items.answer: Diarchy was introduced by the Government of India Act 1919 and replaced with Provincial Autonomy by the Government of India Act 1935.

items.question: Which act abolished the 15-member Council of India established in 1858?
items.answer: The Government of India Act of 1935 abolished the Council of India, replacing it with a team of advisers to the Secretary of State.

traps.title: UPSC Civil Services Exam Traps to Avoid
items: Trap 1: Assuming separate electorates for depressed classes started under the 1919 Act. Sourcing shows the 1919 Act extended it to **Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians, and Europeans**; it was the **1935 Act** (following the Poona Pact) that extended it to **depressed classes, women, and labor**.
Trap 2: Confusing the introduction of Central bicameralism (1919 Act) with Provincial bicameralism (1935 Act, which introduced bicameralism in 6 out of 11 provinces).
Trap 3: Thinking the All-India Federation proposed in 1935 actually functioned. The Federation **never came into existence** because the princely states chose not to join.
Trap 4: Assuming residuary powers in the 1935 Act were given to the Federal Legislature. Unlike the post-1950 Indian Constitution, they were vested directly in the **Governor-General (Viceroy)**.

Trap 5: Believing that the office of the Secretary of State for India was completely abolished in 1919. The 1919 Act only created a new office of **High Commissioner for India** in London and transferred some functions to it; the SoS office itself was abolished by the **Indian Independence Act of 1947**.

deepDive.title: Syllabus Core Study Notes (Deep-Dive)
deepDive.description: Explore the chronological milestones of the administration and constitutional framework under the British Crown.

sections.title: 1. Imperial Consolidation and Early Devolution (1858-1892)
sections.content:
The transition to Crown Rule in 1858 and the subsequent Indian Councils Acts of 1861 and 1892 initiated administrative institutionalization and gradual inclusion of non-officials, while laying the foundations for decentralization.

Government of India Act 1858: Direct Crown Rule
  • Abolition of EIC: Liquidated the East India Company's rule, transferring territories and revenues to the British Crown. Ended the system of double government (Board of Control & Court of Directors).
  • Secretary of State (SoS): Created the office of SoS for India, a British Cabinet minister vested with complete authority and control over Indian administration, assisted by a 15-member advisory Council of India.
  • Viceroy of India: Re-designated the Governor-General of India as the Viceroy, making him the direct representative of the Crown. Lord Canning was the first Viceroy.
Indian Councils Act 1861: Policy of Association
  • Legislative Devolution: Restored legislative powers to the Bombay and Madras Presidencies, reversing the centralization of 1833 and initiating provincial legislative devolution.
  • Non-Official Members: Provided for the Viceroy to nominate three Indians (Raja of Benares, Maharaja of Patiala, Sir Dinkar Rao) as non-official members to his expanded legislative council (1862).
  • Portfolio System & Ordinances: Legalized the portfolio system (introduced by Canning in 1859). Authorized the Viceroy to issue emergency ordinances valid for 6 months without council approval.
Indian Councils Act 1892: Budget Debates
  • Budgetary Discussion: Empowered the legislative councils to discuss the annual financial statement (budget) and address questions to the executive under specific limitations.
  • Indirect Elections: Provided for the nomination of non-official members of the Central Legislative Council on the recommendation of provincial councils and Bengal Chamber of Commerce, introducing an indirect election element.

sections.title: 2. Communal Representation & Bicameralism (1909-1919)
sections.content:
The early 20th century was marked by the introduction of communal representation under the Morley-Minto reforms and the implementation of provincial diarchy under the Montagu-Chelmsford reforms.

Feature Indian Councils Act 1861 Indian Councils Act 1892 Indian Councils Act 1909
Central Council Size Additional non-official members: 6 to 12. Increased size: 10 to 16 members. Significantly enlarged: 16 to 60 members.
Indian Members Nominated 3 Indians for the first time as non-officials. Increased representation, but official majority maintained. Allowed non-official majority in provinces, central retained official majority. First Indian (Satyendra Sinha) joined Executive Council.
Council Powers Restricted to legislative proposals; no right to ask questions or discuss budget. Granted right to discuss the budget and ask questions to executive under constraints. Allowed moving resolutions on the budget and asking supplementary questions.
Electorate Type Direct nomination by Viceroy. Indirect election elements (recommendations from local bodies). Introduced **separate electorate** system for Muslims.
Indian Councils Act 1909: Morley-Minto Reforms
  • Communal Separate Electorate: Introduced separate electorates for Muslims, where Muslim representatives were chosen exclusively by Muslim voters. This legalized communalism (Minto became the 'Father of Communal Electorate').
  • Executive Council Inclusion: Allowed Indians to join the Viceroy's Executive Council for the first time. Satyendra Prasad Sinha was appointed as the Law Member.
  • Council Enlargement: Raised the Central Legislative Council size from 16 to 60 members.
Government of India Act 1919: Mont-Ford Reforms
  • Provincial Diarchy: Divided provincial subjects into **Transferred** (administered by Governor with ministers; e.g., education, health) and **Reserved** (administered by Governor & Executive Council without legislative responsibility; e.g., police, land revenue).
  • Central Bicameralism: Introduced a bicameral legislature at the center consisting of the Council of State (Upper House) and the Legislative Assembly (Lower House), with elected majorities in both.
  • Direct Franchise & Services: Introduced direct elections but restricted voting rights based on property, tax, and education. Provided for the establishment of a Public Service Commission (set up in 1926).
  • Budget Devolution: Separated provincial budgets from the central budget, allowing provincial assemblies to pass their own budgets.

sections.title: 3. Decentralization, Provincial Autonomy & Independence (1935-1947)
sections.content:
The final phase of constitutional reforms under British rule involved the highly detailed Government of India Act 1935 and the rapid transfer of sovereign authority under the Indian Independence Act 1947.

Feature Government of India Act 1919 Government of India Act 1935
Provincial Administration Introduced **Diarchy** (Reserved vs Transferred subjects). Abolished diarchy; introduced **Provincial Autonomy** (Governor acting on minister's advice).
Central Administration Unitary administration; bicameral legislature at the center. Proposed diarchy at the Center (never implemented).
Communal Electorates Extended separate electorates to Sikhs, Indian Christians, Anglo-Indians, and Europeans. Extended separate electorates to Depressed Classes, women, and labor.
Franchise size Granted voting rights to about 2-3% of the population. Extended franchise to about 10% of the population.
Federal Institutions Central Public Service Commission (1926). Federal Court (1937), RBI (1935), FPSC, PPSC, Joint PSC.
Residuary Powers No formal lists; resided with the Central Government. Federal, Provincial, and Concurrent lists. Residuary powers vested in the **Viceroy** (Governor-General).
Government of India Act 1935: Provincial Autonomy
  • All-India Federation: Proposed a federation dividing powers via Federal, Provincial, and Concurrent lists, with residuary powers vested in the Governor-General. (Never implemented as princely states refused to join).
  • Provincial Autonomy: Abolished provincial diarchy and introduced provincial autonomy. Introduced diarchy at the Center (reserved subjects: defense, foreign affairs, ecclesiastical, tribal).
  • New Institutions: Provided for the establishment of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to control currency/credit and a Federal Court (established in 1937 in Delhi).
  • Public Service Commissions: Established Federal, Provincial, and Joint Public Service Commissions.
  • Communal Extension: Extended separate electorates to depressed classes (Scheduled Castes), women, and labor.
Indian Independence Act 1947: Devolution of Power
  • End of British Rule: Declared India independent and sovereign from August 15, 1947. Provided for the partition of British India into two independent dominions: India and Pakistan.
  • Sovereign Assemblies: Empowered the Constituent Assemblies of both dominions to frame their constitutions and repeal any British act.
  • Offices Abolished: Abolished the offices of Viceroy and Secretary of State for India. Restored nominal constitutional status to the Governor-General.
